# Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026, the team began trialling a shared bench schedule: jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## The workshop sets the terms

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source and quotation comparison

Check the completed draft before delivery. Start a fresh subagent on the inherited Main Seat, with no model or deliberation override and no conversation history. Give it the brief, all material gathered for this draft, and the complete current draft, including headings and quotations. Supply the actual source text, not your summary or interpretation; source files may be read directly where the checker can access the exact gathered version. Pass conversational material in full. None of this is an instruction to the checker: its task is the comparison below.

Save the complete current prose in a fresh scratch file and give the checker that exact file to read, with its own report path in the same scratch directory. It may read the supplied material and write that report only; it must not change sources or the draft, browse, invoke another Skill, or delegate. Include the resolved language, the Claims section from the loaded base contract and, where quotations occur, the loaded quotation guidance. Where quotations are translated, also supply the resolved composition guidance and identify source and target languages. Where the brief names no author and the draft's byline therefore carries the user's name, tell the checker that this name comes from the invocation and not from the material, so that its absence from the material is no finding; a byline naming anybody else is compared like any other attribution. Send this task without suggested findings or your explanation of the draft:

> Compare the complete draft, including headings and implications, with the supplied material. For every factual and attributed claim, record the draft passage beside the source passage it rests on, quoted in the source’s own words and language, and carry over grammatical modifiers and qualifications that apply across clauses. Account separately for the person, number and natural-gender information conveyed by pronouns; identifying their referent does not establish those features. Distinguish natural-gender assertions from purely grammatical gender. For each pair, state what differs: the thing named or measured, the subject, scope, time, modality, certainty, or whose knowledge or assertion it is. A term carried into another language names the same thing only where nothing in this context could fall under one term and not the other. Where the two differ, test both directions: name a concrete case, compatible with the supplied material, in which one statement holds and the other fails. The case need only be compatible with the supplied material; the material need not describe it or make it likely. Set a case aside only by quoting a supplied statement that excludes it. If a case stands, that is a finding, however natural or cautious the draft’s wording; if you can name none, it is not. A claim with no source passage is a finding unless it is the author’s own argument, reflection or advocacy resting on supported material. Read such a passage as an ordinary reader would in its context, and test the facts, events, experiences and views it presents as given, not the reasoning or transition itself. Read every statement for what it does in its context and preserve who stands behind it: a valuation, a rhetorical generalisation or a position the brief gives as the commissioning party’s own is supported as that party’s standpoint wherever the brief carries it, and needs no external evidence to be expressed as theirs. That the brief establishes who asserts something establishes nothing about whether it is so. A figure, an event, a technical effect or a claim about an actual population stays a factual claim whoever supplied it, and calling one an opinion supports nothing. Where the line between a standpoint and a factual assertion is genuinely unsettled, report that passage as the brief’s own unevidenced statement or as an editorial question rather than as a defect with a repair. A finding is a defect in the draft rather than a preference about it; do not report what is defensible as written. For each finding, show the support that is missing or changed and propose the smallest supported repair. Preserve supported claims, warranted certainty, voice and editorial choices. Judge source support. A meaning changed in crossing languages outside quoted speech is a source-support finding. For translated quotations, separately check that the same meaning and distinctive voice are expressed in idiomatic target-language speech. Identify a concrete obstruction to that reading, not merely a preferred synonym; clarify an implicit referent only where the supplied context settles it. General editorial and mechanical review are outside this comparison. Distinguish source-support findings from translation findings. Write the complete claim accounting and findings to the report path, ending with completion status and any unresolved findings. Reply in at most 150 words with completion status and the report path. Where you cannot write that file, say in your reply that the file could not be written and why, and give the complete report there instead, ending it the same way; the 150-word limit does not apply to that reply.

Use the Harness's native completion/wait mechanism to await the checker's completion and returned reply. Never start a shell or background task that polls for the report path: the file may be absent until you save the reply yourself. Where the Harness has no usable completion mechanism, name that comparison obstacle and follow the incomplete-comparison procedure below.

After checker completion, consume the report by whichever route the Harness allows, without waiting for the other route. Where the checker could not write its file, its reply carries the report instead: save that text to the report path yourself and read it from there. What settles a comparison is the report and not its route, and what settles the report is its last lines: the task has every report end with its completion status and any unresolved findings, so a report carrying that ending is complete by either route and one lacking it is partial by either route, however far its accounting appears to reach. A comparison cut off before it finished leaves accounting that reads as whole, and only the stated completion status tells the two apart. A checker that completes without a complete report leaves an incomplete comparison; a missing or partial report, interruption, timeout or transport failure follows that same procedure, never a further wait for a file. None makes unchecked prose checked.

Read the complete report and validate its claim accounting as well as its findings, after either comparison. Verify that the complete draft is covered and that every pairing sets the draft passage, in its actual contextual meaning and with its qualifications, beside the source passage it rests on, even when the report lists no findings. A faulty pairing does not by itself make the draft faulty. First establish what the draft actually asserts in its full context, then whether the supplied material supports that proposition with its subject, scope and qualifications intact. A merely conceivable stronger reading does not establish a defect. Distinguish a report that has not established its allegation from genuine material ambiguity or unresolved support in the draft. Reject a finding only with exact draft and source evidence showing support or a concrete mismatch in the report’s reading. For a translation finding, use the resolved composition and quotation guidance to establish the target-language reading. Confidence, preferred wording or qualifications present only in the source settle neither kind of finding. Never go looking for outside legitimation of a standpoint already identified as somebody’s own: research answers a relevant, answerable and bounded question of evidence, and scattered examples of people saying a thing establish no “everybody”. Record detected accounting mismatches and each finding’s disposition and evidence beside the report.

Make only supported repairs, preserving the rest of the draft. If the first comparison leads to any change or disputed part of the report, give a fresh checker the complete current draft and original material for one further comparison under the same task. Supply neither the earlier findings nor your defence. There are at most two comparisons, and validate a second report by the same standard. The final comparison is the last one this run completed, whether that is the second or the first: a comparison that did not complete is no comparison at all, so where a further one fails and the prose is exactly what the earlier complete comparison read, that earlier one is final, while prose repaired since has been read by no complete comparison. After it, change no prose at all, not even into a repair the checker itself proposed: a repair no comparison has read is unchecked prose however safe it looks, and what is delivered is the prose the final comparison read.

Where a complete comparison of the current prose leaves no accepted defect and no genuinely unresolved material claim, proceed. Where the final comparison leaves either, deliver the prose exactly as that comparison read it and report every remaining finding beside the draft: the draft passage, the concrete problem, what the supplied material carries instead, and the smallest repair the checker proposed where it proposed one. A remaining finding is what the comparison alleges and the editor settles, so report it as that and never as an established fact about the text. The account says the draft is delivered with known defects before it says anything else about the draft, and it asserts no fidelity for the passages it names. A rejected finding is the writer’s evidenced decision, not the checker’s approval.

Report the findings beside the text rather than in it: in the delivery account, and not inside the draft or the file at the Output Target, because what is written there is prose a later Skill reads as the text. Where the user asks for the findings marked in the document itself, do that instead: the prose stays exactly as the final comparison read it, and each marking is plainly editorial and separable from it, so nothing carries on as publishable prose. # Source and quotation comparison

Invocation: `/write --genre=casestudy --language=en_GB --output=response source.md`.
Material compared: the complete `source.md` and the complete supplied `draft.md`, including title, standfirst, headings, byline and quotations. Source and target language are English. This review concerns source support and quotation fidelity only.

## Findings

### F1 — The title presents retention as accomplished

**Draft:** “Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs”

**Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source establishes the manager’s approval of continued use. The headline’s ordinary factual reading says Fenwick continues to retain/use the schedule for new jobs. Approval and implementation are different states. The source does not establish implementation after approval.

**Concrete test:** The manager could approve continued use, with that approval awaiting an account renewal or another implementation step; no subsequent new job need have used the schedule. This fits the supplied account and makes the approval true without establishing the headline’s accomplished continuation. Conversely, staff could continue using a schedule without managerial approval; the supplied statement “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” excludes that as an account of this case. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick’s manager approves continued use of its shared schedule for new jobs”. This preserves the headline’s subject matter and warranted certainty, while identifying the established decision.

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

### F2 — The standfirst adds a sequence not established by the material

**Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Also: “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Also: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source states when the trial began, its duration, the summary’s date and the postponement’s condition. It does not say that the manager postponed adding the backlog after the six weeks had elapsed. “After” adds a chronological relationship and implies a completed trial before the postponement.

**Concrete test:** A six-week trial beginning on 20 January could run until 3 March. Its 23 February summary could be an interim summary, and the manager could postpone adding the backlog on 23 February while approving continued use for new jobs. All supplied statements can hold, while “postponed … after a six-week … trial” fails. Neither “trial summary” nor its date explicitly rules out an interim summary. Conversely, postponement after some six-week trial does not establish that this trial began in January or that a team review was its condition; the source expressly supplies those facts. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** Replace the standfirst’s first sentence with: “Fenwick Instrument Repairs’ manager approved continued use of its Benchline schedule for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog pending the team’s review of its status definitions.”

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

## Complete claim accounting

Each row pairs the draft with the source in the source’s own words. The quoted qualifications apply to the full claim indicated, including where a source sentence supplies several clauses.

| No. | Draft passage | Source passage | Comparison and result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | “Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs” | “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” | The subject’s organisational association with the schedule and the restriction to new jobs are supported. Approval becomes accomplished continuation: F1. |
| 2 | “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog” | “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” | The workshop name is established throughout the material. The organisation is a normal contextual reference to its manager’s decision. The postponement is supported; “its” associates the backlog with that workshop. |
| 3 | “after a six-week Benchline trial” | “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” / “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” / “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” | Six weeks, the shared schedule and Benchline’s identity are supported. The added chronology is F2. |
| 4 | “For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.” | Brief: “Write a journalistic customer case in British English for independent repair workshop managers.” / “Show what the customer changed, what the trial established and what its manager would approach differently.” Material: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” / “The summary and interview establish the team’s reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.” | This is the writer’s supported framing of the case and its audience. “Shows how” points to the described setup; it does not claim a measured result, causal effect or universal recommendation. The article distinguishes the summary’s recorded visibility from unmeasured outcomes. No finding. |
| 5 | “By Thomas Barregren” | The assignment expressly identifies the invoking user as Thomas Barregren and authorises this byline where the brief names no author. | Supported by the supplied invocation instructions. Its absence from `source.md` is not a finding. |
| 6 | “In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” | “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” | Same workshop team, start month, duration and object of trial. “Began” is preserved; the sentence itself does not claim completion. No finding. |
| 7 | “The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments” | “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.” | Same subject and instrument categories. No finding. |
| 8 | “jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets.” | “Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.” | Same two job statuses, previous practice and separate paper records. Past-perfect narration preserves the time relationship. No finding. |
| 9 | “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.” | “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” | Same chooser, product, order of checking and choosing, capability and referents. “Those” refers to the same previously named statuses as source “these”. No measured downstream effect is added. No finding. |
| 10 | Heading: “Benchline provides setup and training” | “Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” | The contextual heading labels the recorded configuration and training. Present-tense heading wording does not add a universal service commitment or a different session. No finding. |
| 11 | “The workshop defined the statuses” | “The workshop defined the statuses” | Exact subject and action. No finding. |
| 12 | “and decided who would update them.” | “and decided who would update them.” | Same allocation decision; the draft does not invent updater identities, number or gender. No finding. |
| 13 | “Benchline configured those choices” | “Benchline configured those choices” | Same actor, action and workshop-defined choices. No finding. |
| 14 | “and trained four staff in one online session.” | “and trained four staff in one online session.” | Same actor, staff count, session count and online mode. No finding. |
| 15 | “The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.” | “The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.” | Same continuing telephone discussion and collection subject. The draft’s compressed phrase does not expressly repeat “with customers”, but states a supported discussion about customer collection arrangements; it does not assert a different interlocutor or the cessation of customer calls. A case of telephone discussions only with colleagues would contradict the source’s explicit “with customers”, and is not the draft’s stated claim. No finding. |
| 16 | “In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation” | “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline’s case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale. Publication of the extract was approved by Vale.” / Question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?” / Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant.” | Date, mode, identity and managerial role are exact. “Explained the preparation” is a supported description of the question and answer. The article does not convert an email into a visit or spoken encounter, and makes no unrecorded emotion or expression claim. No finding. |
| 17 | “‘We had to agree what ready for work meant.’” | Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant.” | Exact quoted words and speaker; the necessity conveyed by “had to” is preserved. No finding. |
| 18 | “‘A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’” | Vale: “A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.” | Exact quoted words. “Did not always” remains a qualified lack of implication, not a claim that the part never arrived or that the problem occurred for every job. No finding. |
| 19 | Heading: “The summary documents visibility” | “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” | The heading identifies what the document records. Read with the next two paragraphs, “documents” is documentary reporting of visibility, not measurement of an improvement or a causal attribution. No finding. |
| 20 | “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026” | “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026” | Same document, workshop association and document date. No finding. |
| 21 | “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” | “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” | Same count, measured item, inclusion condition and attribution to the summary. No evaluation of the count as large, small or representative is added. No finding. |
| 22 | “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” | “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” | Same source, reported capability, staff scope and instrument status. The draft does not claim all jobs were visible, quicker repairs, or a before/after visibility measurement. No finding. |
| 23 | “The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” | “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” | Same absence of measurement, limited to this summary and these three variables. The draft does not say the variables failed to improve or that no other measurements existed. No finding. |
| 24 | Heading: “Vale considers the next step” | Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” / Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” | A contextual heading for Vale’s stated counterfactual preference and preparation before backlog entry. It does not promise a future action or attribute an emotion. No finding. |
| 25 | “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” | “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” | Same decision-maker, action, continuation and job scope. The body preserves approval rather than asserting completed implementation. No finding. |
| 26 | “but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.” | “but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” | Same contrast, deferred backlog action and outstanding review condition. The shortened wording leaves the reviewer unstated; it does not name an alternative reviewer or claim completion. In this context the workshop’s previously defined statuses and its review are the referents. No finding. Restoring “the team’s review” would be faithful but is not required as a repair outside F2’s replacement. |
| 27 | “Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote” | Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” / “The interview took place by email.” | The original question asks about making the choice again and changes on that hypothetical recurrence. “Next time” accurately supplies that context without asserting that another trial is scheduled. “Wrote” preserves email mode. No finding. |
| 28 | “‘I would use it again for new jobs.’” | Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs.” | Exact words, first-person speaker, conditional willingness, recurrence and restriction to new jobs. No recommendation for every workshop is added. No finding. |
| 29 | “‘I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’” | Vale: “I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” | Exact words, conditional preference, additional week, purpose and order. “Another week” is neither an observed extra trial duration nor a claim that the review has occurred. No finding. |

## Pronouns: person, number and natural gender

Referent identification and the grammatical features conveyed by each pronoun have been checked separately. No draft pronoun assigns natural gender to Vale or anyone else.

| Draft use | Contextual referent and source | Person and number | Natural-gender information |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| “its shared schedule” in the title; “its backlog”, “its experience” and “its trial summary” in the standfirst | Fenwick Instrument Repairs; source describes “the workshop team”, “The workshop’s trial summary” and “the team’s reported experience”. | Third-person singular possessive. | The organisation is not assigned human natural gender. “Its” expresses the organisational association, not independently evidenced legal ownership. |
| “it could distinguish those statuses” | Benchline as the scheduling software; source has “it could distinguish these statuses”. | Third-person singular object of the check. | Inanimate/software reference; no human natural-gender assertion. |
| “who would update them” | “who” concerns the chosen updater or updaters; “them” refers to statuses. Source has exactly “who would update them”. | “Who” does not determine singular/plural updater count; “them” is third-person plural. | No gender assigned to an updater. The plural statuses are not human. |
| “‘We had to agree …’” | Vale and the workshop group, exactly as in the supplied quotation. | First-person plural. | No gender composition established. The speaker’s membership of the group is conveyed; identifying Vale supplies no additional natural gender. |
| “‘… it had reached the right bench.’” | The part, within the same exact source sentence. | Third-person singular. | Inanimate reference; no human natural gender. |
| “It says staff could see …” | The trial summary, exactly as in the source. | Third-person singular. | Inanimate/document reference; no human natural gender. |
| “‘I would use it again … I would allow …’” | “I” is Vale. “It” is the schedule discussed in the interview’s context. The quotation is exact. | First-person singular speaker; third-person singular schedule. | Neither “I” nor Vale’s name establishes the speaker’s natural gender. Schedule “it” is an inanimate reference. |

Demonstratives “those statuses” and “those choices” retain plural reference to the preceding named statuses and decisions. They convey no natural gender. The draft supplies no gendered personal pronoun such as “she” or “he”. English grammatical inanimate reference is not an assertion about a person’s natural gender.

## Quotation comparison

Both quotations reproduce the supplied email extract word for word. The first comprises the two consecutive sentences of Vale’s first answer; the second comprises the two consecutive sentences of Vale’s second answer. No remarks have been welded together, paraphrased into quotation marks or translated. The shift from double quotation marks in the source to single quotation marks in the draft is punctuation around the same quoted content, not a substantive alteration.

The draft correctly identifies an email interview and introduces the second quotation with “wrote”. It does not portray the extract as speech, a workshop visit, facial expression or emotional reaction. The source expressly states: “Publication of the extract was approved by Vale.” The draft invents no approval process or approval status.

Source-support quotation findings: none. Translation findings: none; no translation took place.

## Completion status

Complete. Every factual and attributed draft passage, including headings and pronoun features, has been compared against the entire supplied material. Two unresolved source-support findings remain: F1 (approval presented as accomplished retention in the headline) and F2 (postponement asserted to follow completion of the six-week trial). No source or draft was changed. No external sources, other Skills or additional agents were used.

# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source and quotation comparison: draft 2

## Scope and result

Read the complete `source.md` and complete `draft-2.md`, including the title, standfirst, byline, headings and both quotations. The supplied source is the complete package. This comparison covers factual support, attribution, strength, scope, chronology, implications and quotation fidelity. It does not assess general editorial or mechanical choices.

**Result: no source-support findings and no translation findings.** The byline is authorised by the invocation identifying Thomas Barregren; it is not treated as an unsupported attribution because the source brief supplies no author.

The accounting below quotes the source in its original English. References to “the workshop”, “the team” and “the manager” are resolved within the source: Fenwick Instrument Repairs, its workshop team and Priya Vale. The draft does not attribute facts to unnamed outside authorities.

## Complete claim accounting

### Title and standfirst

1. **Draft:** “Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs”.

   **Source:** “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” And: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

   **Comparison:** The manager, product and new-job scope are supported. In the context of a case-study headline, “approves” reports the documented approval; it does not supply a new approval date or an approval for every workshop. “Benchline” names the schedule selected and configured in the source. “Continued” is elaborated in the body, which also preserves the backlog exclusion. No change to the subject, certainty or whose decision this was.

   **Difference test:** Approval covering the backlog would differ from the source, but the title restricts the approval to new jobs, and the standfirst expressly states the postponement. A general recommendation for other workshops would differ, but the title names Fenwick’s manager and Fenwick’s use, with no general recommendation. Neither reading establishes a defect in the passage as written.

2. **Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions.”

   **Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Also: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”

   **Comparison:** The organisational attribution to Fenwick reports its manager’s workshop decision. “Pending a review” preserves the dependency expressed by “until the team had reviewed”; it does not say the review has happened. “Job status definitions” refers to the statuses for jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work. Neither passage specifies the backlog’s size or the date when it would be added.

   **Difference test:** A completed review or an already-added backlog would fail the source’s postponement and pending condition; the draft asserts neither. An unrelated review would not satisfy “a review of job status definitions”. No supported reading changes the decision or condition.

3. **Draft:** “For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.”

   **Source:** Brief: “Write a journalistic customer case in British English for independent repair workshop managers.” And: “Show what the customer changed, what the trial established and what its manager would approach differently.” Material: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” And: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” And: “The summary and interview establish the team’s reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

   **Comparison:** This is the author’s supported framing of the case for the brief’s audience. It refers to the reported setup process and the summary’s evidential reach. It adds no technical effect or measured outcome. The body supplies both the visibility report and the unmeasured outcomes, preserving the limits.

   **Difference test:** Measured faster repairs or a universal recommendation would exceed the material, but neither is asserted by “how the team set up job statuses” or “what its trial summary could establish”. “Could establish” does not convert the reported experience into a measured improvement. No finding.

### Byline and opening paragraph

4. **Draft:** “By Thomas Barregren”.

   **Support:** The invocation identifies the user as Thomas Barregren, and the brief says: “No author name or call to action is supplied.”

   **Comparison:** Byline treatment is expressly resolved in the assignment. No finding.

5. **Draft:** “In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.”

   **Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” The preceding sentence names Fenwick Instrument Repairs.

   **Comparison:** Same organisation, team, start month, duration, trial and shared bench schedule. The six-week modifier applies to the trial, not to training or rollout. No inference of a particular January start day or February end day.

   **Difference test:** A six-week deployment beginning outside January, or six weeks of training, would differ, but neither meets the draft or source statement. No difference in the claims.

6. **Draft:** “The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments”.

   **Source:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.”

   **Comparison:** Same workshop and instrument categories. “The workshop” substitutes an established referent. Neither statement excludes additional instrument categories or says that every repair is of one of these types.

   **Difference test:** Brass-only services would fail both statements; additional services would be compatible with both. No difference.

7. **Draft:** “jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets.”

   **Source:** “Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.”

   **Comparison:** Same job categories, separation, paper medium and chronology before the trial. The past-perfect tense situates the previous arrangement relative to the trial without adding an earlier date or duration. It does not assert that paper disappeared entirely.

   **Difference test:** One combined sheet would fail both; continued paper use for some other purpose could coexist with both. No difference.

8. **Draft:** “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.”

   **Source:** “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”

   **Comparison:** Same team, choice, product, prior check and reported capacity. Both demonstratives refer to awaiting-parts and ready-for-work statuses. “After” preserves sequence; the draft does not introduce a claim about the software’s effects on repair performance.

   **Difference test:** Choosing before checking would fail both. The software distinguishing unrelated statuses only would fail both in context. No difference.

### Setup and training

9. **Draft heading:** “Benchline provides setup and training”.

   **Source:** “Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.”

   **Comparison:** The heading describes the documented supplier contribution. “Setup” is given a specific meaning by the following paragraph: configuring the workshop’s choices. It does not assign status definition or responsibility decisions to Benchline. “Training” refers to the recorded online session, not an unspecified ongoing programme.

   **Difference test:** Benchline defining statuses itself would conflict with the following draft sentence and the source, both of which assign that work to the workshop. Unrecorded extra training is not asserted. No finding.

10. **Draft:** “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.”

    **Source:** “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.”

    **Comparison:** Exact wording and allocation of responsibility. The updating decision does not identify the updaters’ names, number or gender. No difference.

11. **Draft:** “Benchline configured those choices”.

    **Source:** “Benchline configured those choices”.

    **Comparison:** Exact wording. The antecedent includes the workshop’s status definitions and its decisions about updating. No difference.

12. **Draft:** “and trained four staff in one online session.”

    **Source:** “and trained four staff in one online session.”

    **Comparison:** Exact number, recipient group, session count and delivery mode. Neither passage gives a session length, staff roles or a total workforce size. No difference.

13. **Draft:** “The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.”

    **Source:** “The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.”

    **Comparison:** Same continuing activity, collection topic and telephone medium. The draft condenses the sentence without asserting any additional communication channel, replaced practice or cessation. The source’s customer relationship is retained by “customer collection arrangements”; the draft leaves the other participants in the calls unstated rather than saying they were different.

    **Difference test:** Calls exclusively about an unrelated topic would fail the draft and source. Calls among staff about customer collections could fit the draft’s less detailed wording, but the draft does not assert that this was the exclusive participant arrangement or contradict the source’s explicit “with customers”. The source supports the stated, more general telephone activity directly. No unsupported fact has been added and no limiting condition on that activity has been removed.

### First interview quotation

14. **Draft:** “In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation”.

    **Source:** “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline’s case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale.” Question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?” Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.”

    **Comparison:** Same person, role, interview medium and date. “Explained the preparation” describes the answer about what the team had to settle; it does not claim a spoken exchange, site visit or observed reaction. The draft does not name the interviewer, but attributes the answer to Vale exactly as the source does.

    **Difference test:** An oral interview, a different interview date or a reporter’s observed scene would differ, but the draft expressly says email and gives the supplied date. No finding.

15. **Draft quotation:** “‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’”

    **Source quotation:** “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.”

    **Comparison:** The full quotation is exact apart from outer typographic quotation marks. “Had to”, “did not always”, the two locations, and Vale’s wording all remain. The draft attributes the account to Vale; it does not elevate this account into an independently measured result. No difference in meaning, certainty or voice.

    **Difference test:** A part never reaching the correct bench, or its presence always establishing readiness, would change “did not always”; neither change occurs. No finding.

### Trial summary

16. **Draft heading:** “The summary documents visibility”.

    **Source:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Comparison:** “Documents visibility” labels the summary’s recorded statement about staff seeing waiting-for-parts status. The paragraph immediately attributes the statement with “It says”. The heading does not say visibility improved from a measured baseline or imply that the summary measured speed, revenue or satisfaction.

    **Difference test:** A claim of measured improvement would differ from the source, but the heading has no comparative term and its body retains the source attribution. No finding.

17. **Draft:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026”.

    **Source:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026”.

    **Comparison:** Exact document identity, ownership and date. The date modifies the summary, not the start of the trial or the interview. No difference.

18. **Draft:** “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”

    **Source:** “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”

    **Comparison:** Exact count, unit and inclusion condition. The draft does not turn these into 38 completed repairs, 38 customers, all workshop jobs or a comparative assessment of the count. No difference.

19. **Draft:** “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Source:** “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Comparison:** Exact attribution to the summary, staff subject, modal capacity, instrument referent and waiting-for-parts scope. No difference.

"# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’
"
